utterances.text: Okay. Anything else about that? You've said that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- if you could answer my questions, because I showed you documents there, and we already talked about pockets of isolated Croats who are threatened and have -- in the middle of a war. Some have to leave. Some go to Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going -- the reason I'm going to this particular book is because this book was introduced by that gentleman, not me, and my question is, when they pointed to a map to you, they didn't point to the other maps, and you haven't bothered to read the whole book, do you think that perhaps before formulating an opinion on what is in the book you should have at least first read it or have it read to you? Do you think that as a very minimum? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I formulated my opinion on a lecture --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] No, no, I'm asking you about --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- of which the book was one of the documents proposed. I have not read the book. I've answered that clearly. My opinion was formed by the lecture which Mr. Anto Valenta gave me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Sir, I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- in which he showed me those maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, now, could you answer my question? That's why I asked you if you ad anything else to supplement. See, I'm fair to you. I want you to be fair to the Judges, because we have precious time. Do you think you should have read the book before commenting on the book that was shown to you, because that's what you did when you were commenting to that gentleman's question as he was pointing that out to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution never requested the witness to comment on the contents of the book. Simply, the maps were shown or the maps on page 43 and page 66 were shown to the witness, and with a question, were these the maps or were these of the maps that you were shown. That was all. He was not requested to comment on the contents of the book. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously the witness doesn't wish to cooperate here and so therefore there is no need --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point too, because this is ridiculous. Mr. Karnavas has completely mischaracterised the witness's testimony on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] What he's saying is, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to finish my objection. The witness is not being treated fairly on this. The witness's testimony quite clearly was that he had a meeting with Mr. Valenta. During the meeting with Mr. Valenta, Mr. Valenta stated certain views and talked to-- had a conversation with the witness, which the witness has related to us. The witness never purported at any time, either on direct examination or on examination, cross-examination, that he had read the book; never said that, in fact, plainly to the contrary. In the course of the discussion and meeting with Mr. Valenta, the witness said he had seen -- that Mr. Valenta had shown him certain maps as -- simply as a vehicle to ask the witness if the kind of maps in the back of his book were the kind of maps that were shown to him during this meeting. The witness confirmed those were the sort of maps, with arrows and big movements, that were shown to him. Now, that's the full scope of the witness's testimony on his meeting with Mr. Valenta. He didn't express a view on Mr. Valenta or Mr. Valenta's book. So all this character -- mischaracterisation and misstatement of the record by Mr. Karnavas is completely improper and not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we have to finish, because it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may with one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were shown a map that was on page 43. It was map 17. Do you recall being shown that map by Mr. Kruger?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that map in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know who generated that map or where that map came from?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to -- to find out that everything that is in the books, all -- with the exception of the maps that Mr. Valenta draws himself, the other maps, come from open sources and this particular map comes from a Muslim source? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that and, yes, it is a little bit surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's surprising that you didn't read the book before forming an opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that I need to go to footnote 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Look at 1D 01538. This is the footnote that is accompanying the text right after -- right before we see the map. This is the source. It's -- did you ever hear of this text, Bosanski Pogledi?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that but I don't recognise it on the screen either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you see the date? It's on footnote 59, sir. If you look at my text, what I copied, 1D 01538.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at that document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the back, you'll see we've listed, we had it typed out or printed out, and this is a publication, a periodical, that's published, I'm told, by Zulfikarpasic, who is a renowned Bosnian intellectual who is currently living in Sarajevo. And also look at footnote 35. Were you aware of these publications, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of these publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because if you look at -- if you look at source 35, for instance, maps of 15, 16, and 17, these were the maps that were -- some that were in the book, they come from this particular source, and if you look at the table of contents you will see where the sources -- what sources Mr. Valenta is relying on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have a 20-minute break we will reconvene in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. During the break I have been informed of the time used and left. The Petkovic Defence has one hour and 50 minutes left. The Coric Defence has 20 minutes left. The Pusic Defence has 25 minutes. The Praljak Defence one hour and a half, and the Stojic Defence 40 minutes. Who is going to start for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Watkins, good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good day to my learned friends and everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, I wish to say at the outset that the time that you have given to General Petkovic is more than sufficient for us, and according to my plan, we will give some of our time to the Defence of General Praljak. I hope that I will be able to clarify certain points with Mr. -- with the witness in about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, I would like us to clarify part of a Prosecution document that you commented on. That is P 06303 in the Prosecutor's set of documents. That is daily summary for the 31st of October, where there is reference to a meeting with Mr. Prlic, and his words concerning Stupni Do are conveyed, that General Petkovic, the Chief of Staff of the HVO, stated that he had removed all the local commanders and that an investigation had been started.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is all I have to say about the document. Let us now try to analyse this statement by Mr. Jadranko Prlic -- or, rather, the part of the document quoting his words. First of all, let us see whether in October 1993 General Petkovic was actually the Chief of Staff of the HVO as mentioned in this document. Mr. Watkins, you told us that you had spoken to General Praljak in August 1993, and that he had told you that he, Praljak, was the commander of the HVO. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. He said he was the Supreme Commander of the HVO, and added that General Petkovic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also told us, Mr. Watkins, that in November there was a change at the head of the HVO and that General Praljak was replaced by General Roso. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to conclude from this that at the end of October 1993, General Petkovic was not at the head of the HVO but that, rather, it was General Praljak who was at the head of the HVO at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was our understanding. You'll remember on Monday we were discussing trying to find out who was in command and when, but that is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In my set of documents, which is before you on the desk, could you please look at P 06091.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The date is the 25th of October, 1993, the Srednja Bosna military district in Vares. It is delivered by Brigadier Zarko Tole, as one can see at the bottom of the document, and he is said to be the chief of the Main Staff of Herceg-Bosna. So on the basis of this, we can conclude that the chief of the Main Staff was Brigadier Zarko Tole. Can we agree on this fact?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall a document on Monday where I went to Citluk to the headquarters and I met Brigadier Tole, and certainly in my mind there was -- it was unclear as to the exact order of command. From what you're saying here in terms of this document, it would suggest that Brigadier Tole on the 25th of October was the Chief of Staff, but it appears that General -- sorry, Jadranko Prlic told me that it was Petkovic who was dealing with the issue of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, could you perhaps explain to us what the letters OZ and GS which are -- figure before the word "Main Staff" signify?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are abbreviations for Main Staff of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The army of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina bore this official title, armed forces, and this is pursuant to the decree establishing this body, but many documents use the abbreviation HVO to refer to the same body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would now like us to see whether anyone in the Main Staff, whether the Chief of Staff or the commander, had the authority to replace or dismiss any commander, and this has to do with what you quote as Mr. Prlic's words that General Petkovic said he had removed all the local commanders. So could you look at 4D 00521, which is a decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the consolidated text from November 1993, and please look at Article 34. The Chamber is familiar with this article, so while you are serving for it, I will say that according to this decree commanders in the armed forces were appointed or dismissed or relieved first by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, referring to brigade commanders and higher-ranking officers, while other officers, lower at -- lower-level officers, non-commissioned officers, and others, were appointed and relieved by the head of the defence department. Mr. Watkins, were you familiar with the rules and regulations governing appointments in the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of these articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we conclude -- based on this article, and no other article of this decree refers to appointing and relieving commanders, so could we conclude that nobody in the Main Staff was able to appoint or relieve commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Back to speculation, Your Honour, and I'm just concerned that we're going down a road where we're going to have just a series of reading documents to the witness, and we're back to, did I read the document correctly. So unless there is some foundation for how this witness can express a view on these matters, I think -- I think we're wasting -- we'll be wasting a lot of time. But beyond -- my initial objection is, this is purely speculative and goes beyond the face of the document to ask this witness whether anyone else on the Main Staff could take any sort of action, to expect any sort of discipline in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not share your view on that point, Mr. Scott. Here we have a document produced by the witness stating that Mr. Prlic told him that General Petkovic had removed a number of officers. The Defence, using Article 4 -- 34, on the basis of Article 34 states that the head of the Main Staff did not have the power to remove anyone. It's the heart of the matter, really. If I was conducting the proceedings, I would have put the question in a different way. So what really matters here is the way the question has been put. You should ask the witness whether what he wrote is not in contradiction with the applicable law, and then you should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this suggestion, Your Honour. I fully accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the witness then ask the question is asked by His Honour Judge Antonetti as if I had put it. In other words, from this article that you have just read in this decree, does it follow that what Mr. Jadranko Prlic is said to have said here does not correspond to the legislation then in force?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, reading this quickly, that it would correspond, and if I could just note that the second sentence of Article 34 says: "Commanders of brigades and high-ranking officers shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the Defence Department or by commanders appointed by him." I understand that the individuals involved in Vares was Ivica Rajic, who was a brigade commander. I would suggest that from this second sentence that the commander appointed by the defence department could remove a brigade-level commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the third time now when analysing this article, we have a problem with the way it has been edited. Without going into an in-depth analysis, I wish to point out that the president of the HZ HB appoints commanders of brigades and high-ranking officers, while all lower-level officers are appointed by the defence department or by commanders appointed by him. So the problem is in the way this article has been edited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in any case does it follow from this article that the Main Staff would be authorised to appoint or relieve any military commander?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of the text in front of me here is that, yes, and commander appointed by the head of the defence department could remove a brigade-level commander. That's all I can see. My interpretation is, yes, that they could, and that would be standard -- well, it wouldn't be inconsistent with other military structures that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this article give the Main Staff any kind of authority?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where is the Main Staff mentioned here? We are referring to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So tell me, where is the Main Staff mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of the staff are not mentioned here. It is the commanders of the brigades, and the ability of a commander of the brigade to be appointed by another commander who has been appointed by the head of the defence department. I can only interpret what I'm reading here, and I've not seen this before, as I've said. To me, this document would allow General Petkovic or Tole or Praljak to remove a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't have time to go into a detailed analysis with you now, but please tell me, in spite of the fact that you are erroneously applying to the head of the defence department, these authorities, would the Main Staff solely on the basis of this decree, without receiving any authorisation from the defence department be able to do this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation is, yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Without the authority of the head of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be something lost in translation. I'm reading an English version, and all I can say is that the second sentence to me reads very clearly, that, "a commander of a brigade and high-ranking officers shall be appointed or replaced by the head of the Defence Department ..." The question you're asking is for me to stop reading at that point. If I didn't read the next few words, I would agree with you. But the next few words say: " ... or by commanders appointed by him." So he has delegated that authority to commanders appointed by him, is the way that I would interpret this. I can offer nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, it really is a mistranslation, so I will not dwell on this. We will clarify certain points using other documents. Please look at document P 00280. This is an order issued by Mate Boban, dated the 27th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of June, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. This is a commander, whom you referred to as the commander of the Central Bosna area. Is that correct? The year is 1992?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was commander of operative zone middle Bosna, above a brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You explained that communication in Central Bosnia was very difficult because there were certain pockets controlled by the HVO, and communication between those pockets as well as communication with the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander was very difficult. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, did you know that precisely for this reason Mr. Tihomir Blaskic had far greater powers compared to commanders of other operative zones?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that he had any extra or additional powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document we have just opened, P 00280, and look at paragraph 2, which says: "The main commander appoints the commander of the sector of HVO Central Bosnia, and is fully responsible for full articulation." Did you know that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was authorised to appoint and relieve all commanders of military units in the Central Bosna area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that in legal terms, but it wouldn't surprise me that he had that capability.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look for the sake of illustration documents P 00765 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just probe a bit into this? Mr. Witness, the decree which we had seen before, could you give us the date of that decree? It was 00521, 4D 00521.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, at the top of the document it says 17 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And when -- what's the date of the order we are looking at now, 00280?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That order, sir, is the 27th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of a degree, with what rules applied at that time to the nomination or dismissal of commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just a brief point of clarification. The decree I showed, which was published in October 1992, is the consolidated text, which means that there was a piece of legislation that had been enacted earlier. It was modified in the meantime, and then the modifications have been entered into the text, which then becomes the consolidated text. I didn't want to put to the witness this whole sequence of documents, but the decree was actually enacted in June 1992, so that between this order issued by Mr. Boban and the structure of Herceg-Bosna, there is no inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, we are now dealing with document P 00765, from which it can be seen that it is an order issued by Tihomir Blaskic as the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, and he's appointing the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, and he is appointing Mr. Emil Harah. This documents shows that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was in fact authorised to appoint brigade commanders in his area and that he actually did so. Is this correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document would suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see whether this was the case later on when this conversation with Mr. Prlic took place. Let's look at document P 06000. This is an appointment dated the 22nd of October, 1993. Colonel Tihomir Blaskic is appointing the brigade commander of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, and the person appointed is Mario Bradara. Can we agree, Mr. Watkins, that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was equally authorised in October to appoint and relieve the commanders of military units in the Central Bosnia area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hesitate for just one reason. It -- I just want to be clear on the date of this document. It's the -- yeah. Sorry. Yes, this would appear to suggest that. I -- could I just make a point, sir? I'm little concerned or unsure and it refers to an earlier document. I'm not sure I'm able to do this under document 280 to which I was earlier referred, it says that -- am I allowed to -- can I carry on? 280. We have a document dated, "Grude, 27th of June, 1992." And yet the name at the bottom is General Anto Roso, and I was unaware of his presence in 1992. I just don't understand that. That's the only thing I mention about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you have no reason to doubt that Mr. Roso was there in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know. I was just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at P 06000. In the left lower part one can see that Colonel Tihomir Blaskic only delivered this document as information to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the introductory part, which is the same as the one in the order of 1992. Does Tihomir Blaskic refer to the decree on the armed forces and the authority of the Supreme Commander? And the date he refers to is the 27th of June, 1992. We can look at this document, and you will see that this is document number 396/93 of the 27th of June, 1992, which is the document we have just seen, P 00280. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that reference is made.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, did you ever have any knowledge, did you ever see any document authorising someone, or a document in which somebody else apart from Tihomir Blaskic appointed or relieved any commander of any military units in the Central Bosnia area from June 1992 until the Washington Accords when Mr. -- or, rather, during the period when Mr. Tihomir Blaskic was the commander there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The third part of Mr. Jadranko Prlic's statement, if it is correctly conveyed here, says that an investigation had been instituted as regards the events in Stupni Do. So let's look at a few documents together. 4D 00500. This is a document issued by the deputy military prosecutor of the -- it's dated the 28th of June, 1993. That is five days after Stupni Do, and it asks the HVO Bobovac Brigade for certain information as to whether any crimes had been committed in the municipalities of Vares and Kakanj. Mr. Watkins, did you have any knowledge about the role of the military prosecutor's office as regards the gathering of information relative for criminal proceedings and the instituting charges against persons accused of war crimes and other crimes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was merely reporting that an investigation was under way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at all the dimensions of that investigation and attempts made by the organs of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna to have something done about it. Look at document P 06842 next, please. It's a letter by the head of the president's office, Mr. Vladislav Pogarcic to the Ministry of Defence and Mr. Perica Jukic. Mr. Watkins, if I understood you correctly in your testimony, you knew both Vladislav Pogarcic and Minister Perica Jukic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this letter we can see that the -- that President Boban's office is asking the minister of defence to supply a detailed report about the events in Stupni Do, and in the passages to follow they say what information they want, the names, surnames, the suspects, the fact that the Geneva Conventions might have been violated, et cetera, et cetera. So from this letter, would it emerge from that the presidential office and the ministry of defence were included in the attempts made to establish the truth about the events in Stupni Do and to unleash proceedings to find the perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Both the Presidency and the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at another document. 4D 00506 is the number. And the Trial Chamber has already seen this document, but I think it would be a good idea to hear your opinion and to hear whether you knew of attempts made by Perica Jukic, the Defence Minister, with the assistance of UNPROFOR, to all the information supplied about individuals who were suspects, who were suspected of having perpetrated the crime in Stupni Do. And you can see the names here which are listed, Ilijasevic, Ljoljo, Rajic, Bakula, et cetera. Now, did you know the attempts made by the top organs of Herceg Bosna to receive information from international organisations and their assistance of uncovering the perpetrators of these unlawful acts or crimes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more document about that, please, and it is 4D 00499. It is a document from the commander for SIS of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade to the district military prosecutor in Travnik. Tell us, please, Mr. Watkins, do you know what SIS stands for? The abbreviation SIS, do you know which service that was? It is the security and information service, in fact. You know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You answered before you gave me the chance to say the same. It's the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you aware of the role and tasks of that same service in gathering information relevant to legal proceedings or criminal proceedings to be initiated?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. They had this task, as does the regular police force with respect to criminal proceedings before civil courts. From this document we can see that the SIS of the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade is sending to the military prosecutor's office, district military prosecutor's office, people who were suspects up until then of having committed the crime in Stupni Do, and other documents that they considered to be relevant. Now, since you did not know the place and role of the SIS in criminal proceedings before the military prosecutor's office, I'm not going to ask you any special questions with regard to that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question from me. I'm having a look at this document, and I can see that there is an attachment to the letter sent to the military prosecutor, the written statement of Marinko Ljoljo and Marinko Jurisic are attached. These may be of interest, and these have not been attached to your document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have prepared these statements, as well as a document which is the third document mentioned in the first section of this letter; however, I did not expect this witness to know about the details of the investigation conducted so that I did not prepare those documents within my set of documents, because I hadn't intended to present them to this witness, but I'm sure there will be an occasion to do so in due course and we shall be doing that in the proceedings that follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Watkins, on the basis of these documents, would it be right to conclude, and we've already said this in part, that the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Ministry of Defence, the military prosecutor's office, the security and information service or intelligence service, were actively included in the gathering of relevant information and in launching criminal proceedings against the perpetrators of these crimes in due course in Stupni Do? Or let me put it this way: Can we take it that that is the investigation you talked about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation I talked about was simply referring to the fact that Jadranko Prlic told me General Petkovic was instigating a report. The documents that you've presented to me today show the full panoply and range of people involved with that. All I can say is that Jadranko Prlic told me that General Petkovic was instigating it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May I just draw your attention, at least that is what the B/C/S text says, Mr. Prlic did not tell you that Petkovic had instigated the investigation, but it just says that an investigation was instigated without specifying who. P 0633 -- 03 is the document we're talking about. It doesn't emerge that Petkovic actually instigated the investigation. It's neutral. It doesn't say who. It says it was instigated, and that was not within his remit to do so.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is true. It says that Stupni -- sorry, with regard to Stupni Do, he, and that is Jadranko Prlic, stated that General Petkovic, Chief of Staff, had removed all local commanders, and an investigation was under way. I agree that the -- an investigation could be neutral. It could be other people. But what's clear is General Petkovic removed the commanders. The other bit, I agree, is neutral in the way it's presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Watkins, if General Praljak was the commander of the armed forces, and if Mr. Tole was the chief of the Main Staff, what post did General Milivoj Petkovic occupy then?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending exactly on the timings, this is where we were unsure so I'm just reporting obviously at this moment Jadranko Prlic considers that General Petkovic is making the dismissals, and I was unsure, as I've said before, exactly who was in ascendance at any one point. But the fact that I've included after his name General Petkovic Chief of Staff, my understanding on the date that I wrote that report was that that was his key role. As of 31st of October. So General Praljak -- in my mind, on the 31st of October, the order of command was General Praljak, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see, Mr. Watkins. Thank you for your answers. And now I'd like us to move on to another topic, to talk about Central Bosnia and the war events in Central Bosnia. Now, to start off, let us take a look at a Prosecution documents which is in my set of documents, in my binder. It is P 02750, and it is a document from UNPROFOR in which they assess and analyse the events that took place on the territory of Central Bosnia in mid-June 1993, which is to say the time of your arrival in the area of Travnik, and I assume this will be something you know about. We have read the document extensively in this courtroom, and now I'd like to avoid any repetition and ask you to focus on the addendum, the attachment, which in the English text is on page 10, page 10 of the English. And in the B/C/S it is on page 12. And let us look at the heading: "Military consequences," that passage. And "UNPROFOR assesses that the Muslim community was isolated and it cannot survive on its own, that its energy sources and economic sources have been exhausted, that this has no open routes for passage generally and for the bringing in and taking out of resources and fuel." And I skip a sentence it. It says: "The BH army must seek a solution of its own." And now an important sentence we come to and I'm going to quote that. "It will try and clean up all the communities of Ilidza in the central triangle, Travnik, Vares, and Kiseljak, that triangle." Now I'd like to skip over points 1, 2, and 3 or you can read them quickly to yourself, and it goes on to say: "The Muslims have realised that control if routes is a key to solving their problem. They will probably attempt to push south to Prozor from Travnik. They have also realised that control of Jablanica and Konjic is critical." Tell me, please, Mr. Watkins, whether this assessment you consider to be a realistic one, or is your assessment of the events that took place in Central Bosnia in mid-June 1993 different?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have written it like this. I think I would have a slightly different perspective. There are elements in there I wouldn't disagree with, but just quickly, and you'll appreciate this is the first time I've looked at the document, the Croats in Southern Bosnia and South-central Bosnia will probably become even more hostile towards future Muslim convoys attempting to reach the coast -- I'm sorry, the little bit that you referred to me about pushing south from the pocket, I'm just trying to find that now. If I can refer to your text. "They will continue to push south from Prozor to and from Prozor to Travnik, Jablanica, and central ..." Could you refer where you state that on line 7? Could you point to that in the document for me? It will help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't mention line 7 of the document, and I wasn't able to follow the transcript at the same time so I'm not sure what you're referring to. I didn't mention any line 7. I didn't refer to line 7 in those terms. But on page 10 -- Mr. Watkins, can you tell me again what you're actually asking me?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the monitor that I have in front of me, we have your questions and my answers, and on line 7 you are referring to what HVO forces might do, and I'm just saying, could you refer to me in a document where that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, it's not the intentions of the HVO forces but the intentions of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and on page 10, point 2 of the section titled Military Consequences, A, we read out the introduction, the introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I found all the elements that I need. My assessment of what was happening in Central Bosnia with regards to the Muslims wanting to clear out the pockets, I wouldn't agree with that. What they certainly wanted to do was open new routes and we saw evidence of that. They wanted to connect Zenica to Travnik, and we saw them in open conflict with HVO in Travnik where the armija forces were successful. But having pushed them into the pockets, it would have taken an enormous military capability to have beaten the HVO in the Vitez pocket, and equally the HVO in the Vitez pocket, as referred to in this document suggesting that they might push south to Prozor, is a completely unrealistic statement of the capability of the HO -- HVO forces. As I said previously, they had no offensive capability, and what we actually saw in Vitez was them in protective pockets and able to sustain a defensive ring which was being probed all the time, but they didn't have an offensive capability to break out of those pockets and move south. Any connection between Central Bosnian forces and other forces in Herzegovina would have had to come from Herzegovina, and, as indicated before, would need some additional resources beyond that and capability beyond that that we'd seen with the HVO. So I don't think that the HVO assessment is quite right and I don't think that the armija assessment is quite right, but I do understand why they might have written it. That's all I -- yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I want to draw your attention to the fact that this breakthrough towards the south was assessed as being a BH army plan, but I don't want to dwell on that any more because I don't have enough time, but I have prepared a number of maps to show you, and they give us a visual overview of the situation in Central Bosnia and the south sections to Jablanica and Konjic. So would you now please look at document 4D 00561, and it shows the situation in Central Bosnia for March and April 1993. And, in April, you were in the Gornji Vakuf area and the surrounding parts. So perhaps you will be familiar with the situation. But tell me this: Did you know that at that time the axis of -- attacked by the BH army is was as is indicated on the map and the places of conflict was the areas between Jablanica and -- and Gornji Vakuf and Zenica? I assume being find your way on this map and that I don't need to explain it in any detail. I'd just like to ask you whether that was what the situation was like, to the best of your knowledge, or was it different?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This broadly reflects the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at the next document. 4D 00562 is the number. And it shows the situation in June, June 1993. And tell me once again whether this reflects the situation as to the BH army axes and the areas in which the conflict took place, and does it correspond to what you knew about the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not a very good map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is not good on it, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states that in June 1993 there were HVO control up through as far as Bugojno. In fact, it wasn't much beyond Prozor. And if you look at Travnik, we'd had major fighting in Travnik, and a the HVO forces were no longer in Travnik, and so the pocket is very different there. But the arrow which you see coming from Zenica towards Travnik is that very thrust I mentioned earlier, an attempt to connect Zenica to Travnik. So by this time we actually have armija forces controlling Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell it us, please, and we're referring to June 1993, whether it is true and correct that it was precisely in that month that the HVO lost control of the area or, rather, that the BH army took control of Bugojno, Travnik, Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true to say that the situation completely changed between the beginning of June and the end of June, and that -- if this date on here was 1 June, I would be less critical of it. If it's 3-0 June, it's very inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to ask the witness something linked to this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that your superior, Mr. Thebault, on the 10th of June, attended a meeting where I myself and Mr. Delic were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised, because he was one of the signatories of our talk. Now, do you know that the BH army, up until the 15th of June, completely took control of the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I'm saying that this is not a very good map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here we see the intent. The next map will show you that Travnik was not under HVO control, so this shows, and my counsel showed you, the intentions of the BH army in June, and you confirmed that because it -- the thrust of the attack was from Zenica towards Travnik, and you confirmed that. Now, let me go on to ask you this: If we're looking at June as a whole, then you can't claim that the HVO did not have -- or did not exist in Bugojno. Would that be correct or not? Or, rather, do you know that in June the HVO was still in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I met the commanders in there, and I was actually there when the headquarters of the HVO Brigade was evacuated under the fighting and they moved south. I forget the exact dates, but I was actually in the HVO headquarters in Bugojno when it was evacuated. I, with references to other documents, could give you an exact date of that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're talking about Bugojno, but I think you've got it wrong by one month, and I'll show you that later. So what you're -- what you're talking about Bugojno is correct, but it happened in July.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say I needed to look at the dates. I was in Travnik when we set up the communication -- the coordination centre in Travnik, and also we were evacuated there. Now, that was certainly in the period of this map, and so the large blue area indicated by HVO would be correct at the beginning of June. It would be wrong at the end of June, and I can't state what this -- when this map -- whether it refers to the beginning or the end. It was a very fluid period as you know, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Witness. I think we've dealt with that misunderstanding, and this shows the situation up until the 15th of June, when the BH army took full control of Travnik by an attack from Zenica, as you said, and I'm going to let my counsel continue now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Watkins, this map is designed to show what battles took place in June, and I think we've dealt with that. Let's look at the next document now 4D 005673 is the number and it shows the situation in July 1993. So can we see on the basis of this map that Bugojno, Travnik, Novi Travnik is in the green area, which means that the BH army had taken control of these towns and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a -- yes. This map is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the map after the war operations in June. We saw what happened in June earlier on. Now let's look at the it next document, 4D 00564, and we are now -- we've now come to September 1993. To the best of your knowledge, does this map reflect the places where the conflict took place during that month?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is accurate. Zepce, I would want to refresh my mind, but concentrating on the Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak pockets and around Gornji Vakuf; I would say this is accurate. I went to Zepce on the 4th of September, and that's why I question these particular front lines. I can't remember exactly what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this map there's a mistake. Kakanj is the mistake. At that time in June of that year, Kakanj no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but Kakanj is in the green area. Kakanj is shown here in the green area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next month, and the document is 4D 00565, and it shows us the situation for October 1993, that is to say the month when you left and went to Mostar in mid-October, but perhaps you know about the war events in that month of October, and is this map accurate? Does it correspond to your recollections?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and we see that the Kakanj pocket's gone. My inclination is with General Praljak, that in the previous one that might have been one error.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's not deep into the green area, but it is there in June. Now I'm not going to ask you about the events of November 1993, but we could take a look together at another map which shows us the situation in November 1993, and it shows all the places which came under the control of the BH army during the months that you were there. So let us now take a look at document 4D 00567. It is a document which we included into our binder subsequently today. It is to your left, Mr. Watkins, the one document on its own.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We added it -- that on later on, and we apologise to the Judges because we did not include it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, this shows the situation in November 1993, and we can see there that for the period we're discussing that the BH army took control of the following places, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Fojnica, Kakanj, Vares came later, and the area around Zenica. Tell us now, please, Witness, to the best of your recollections, is this map accurate? Does it reflect what actually happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, but you did make reference to Vares happening later, so we -- you would suggest there was an inaccuracy there yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In November -- in November 1993. I was referring to a period after the period you were there. Mr. Watkins, there are some numbers mentioned here next to each of those places. Could you tell us what these numbers might mean? Would those be Croats from those towns who, because the HVO lost control of the area, left for some other areas?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before I answer that question, what I haven't clearly got in my mind is the origin of the maps and who is issuing them. That would then help me to explain what those numbers might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There are numerous sources of maps, but these maps have been prepared by the Defence of Generals Petkovic and Praljak, the two Defence teams together.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that this is probably relating to number of Croats that were either in the pockets or affected by the pockets. So, for instance, the figure of 9.000, which appears to be linked to Vares, we know and referred to earlier documents of, I think, 5 or 6.000 people coming out of Vares. So I would say it is probably an indication of -- of Croats in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And one further question, Mr. Watkins. If I remember correctly, you tried to explain to us that the authorities of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar were dissatisfied with the military situation in Central Bosnia. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I just have one question, a follow-up question, actually. I followed with great interest those maps which are very eloquent, because we can see the evolution on the ground as of the month of June up until October. I notice, while BiH was gaining terrain, I notice that there is an existence of a pocket of Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca. You were on the ground. You had access to military data. How do you explain the fact that the HVO was able to maintain itself in that area while it is -- or while they were completely circled by the ABiH? Is there a military reason? Did they have a lot of weapons? Is it because of bunkers? Is it because of the configuration of the terrain? Is there a reason that can explain this, while the BiH is taking more and more ground, there is that access Travnik-Vitez-Busovaca that is maintained. It could also apply to Kiseljak that we can call a pocket as well, but is there a reason, or how can you explain this? Or is this a question that I should ask another witness, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could give you my attempts if that helps. We -- broadly speaking it would correspond with where there were large population settlements of Croats. So you have particularly in the Lasva Valley, which is the area running from Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, and through down to Kiseljak. And as the BiH had military successes, the forces that were, for instance, in Bugojno would have moved south. Those that were in Travnik would have gone into Vitez. So what you're actually having is a concentration of Croat population living there anyway, and that concentration being reinforced by defeat. So in fact you're getting a redistribution of HVO forces, and a moment has come where the front lines settle, where there is enough military capability in that pocket to - sorry, Your Honour, I'm going to fast - where there is enough military capability to defend those borders -- that front line, rather. So an initial concentration and then -- of population, and then as forces are defeated in other areas, they begin to concentrate in those pockets. So you get to a state where the armija may have wanted to have taken more territory, but there was enough capability to -- to defend those particular lines. They didn't have any particular extra weapon capability there, and the majority of the equipment that we saw would be small arms and mortars. I don't ever recall seeing a tank, a T-54 or T-55 in, for instance, the Vitez pocket, but did see them up in the Zepce pocket. So they had slightly different arrangements there. In fact, what was interesting about the one I saw in Zepce is it had Cyrillic markings on it, and this was a deal that had been done with the Serb forces. So the pockets of Zepce that had a connection with the Serb front line had a different weapon capability, and we would also see that in Kiseljak where I personally witnessed a cooperation between the Croat forces and the Serb forces in movement. But broadly speaking, we are talking about a not particularly well-equipped HVO broadly relying on a concentration of population and the forces all being -- all the population being mobilised to defend that area. I hope that helps, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We may have the opportunity to get back to this in the future. Who will continue now?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to inform the Chamber that the Defence of Mr. Coric has no questions to put to this witness, so we have given the 20 minutes -- 20 minutes of our time to Mr. Prlic's Defence and 20 to Mr. Praljak's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We do not have many questions for this witness, only a few, just in order to clarify some points made by the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Watkins.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when questioned by my learned friend about a document drawn up by you, if you recall it's the special report on the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, dated the 8th of November, 1993. It's P 06381. I don't know whether you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a report compiled by you, and you explained to us how you came by the information included in it. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And it is assessed as an excellent report, which we can see from the preamble of the document. We have the preamble here. You provide some details concerning the structure of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the various organs of government. You mention some names. You didn't who the minister would be. You explained all this yesterday, but let's go back to point 7, which we discussed yesterday. As it says here, it refers to the recently established instruments of government of the HZ HB including four decrees and republican institutions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, not decrees, interpreter's correction, but offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Four offices are mentioned here, office of legal affairs, office of international cooperation, and immigration office of refugees and displaced persons, and office of information, and you said that Mr. Pusic was probably to be at the head of the office of the refugees and displaced persons, but then you corrected yourself and said that you were probably wrong.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have not in this report put Mr. Pusic's name against any appointment. There were several candidates. Another one would have been Martin Raguz, but I'm speculating now and I didn't speculate at the time when I wrote this report. I reason I mention those two names, if it helps, is whenever we were dealing with humanitarian issues or movement of people or prisoner of war exchanges, either Mr. Pusic or Mr. Martin Raguz were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when you look at point 7, you see that the title or the name of the organ that Mr. Pusic was at the head of is the service for the exchange of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So the structure that you mention is not present here. This is not mentioned among these various offices and an institutions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Mr. Pusic's function at the time and when I was dealing with him is not mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the record, Your Honour, I was referring to Prosecution document P 03191, the decision on establishing the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons headed by Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid speculation, could you please take a look at this document, which is also before you, and that's number P 07005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have said that you had been looking at document P 03191. Was to not, rather, document P 06381.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite, Your Honour. It was only for the sake of the record that I said that P 03191 is the government decree -- or the decision of the government of Herceg-Bosna appointing Mr. Pusic at the head of the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. I did not, however, wish to put this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you need not look for the document, Witness. Would you please, rather, look at the document before you, P 07005, in order to avoid speculating who was at the head of the office for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is more or less the time when you arrived in Mostar. I think you arrived on the 17th of October, 1993. Would that being correct? And Mr. Raguz who until then had been the deputy head of the office was now appointed head of the office of displaced and refugees.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this document states, as of 1st of December. When I was dealing with Mr. Pusic first of all that would have been end of October and his title then was -- I forget the exact first title but it was prisoner of war exchange. I can't remember. It was officer of -- it wasn't a minister. It was an appointment, but here as of the 1st of December it does clearly state that Martin Raguz is dealing with the office of the expelled, displaced, and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And from the same document we can see that Mr. Darinko Tadic preceded him in that post. I don't know whether you had occasion to meet Mr. Tadic. And Mr. Raguz had previously been his deputy?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not meet Mr. Tadic, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You have another document before you, P 00846. It is the decision on the establishment of the office for expelled persons, refugees, and displaced persons. It was published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then I apologise and I will not ask you any questions about it. If you don't have the document, I will not put any questions about this, but I will ask you: The office that Mr. Martin Raguz was in, his task was to deal with all matters concerning refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, there were the two people that we needed to talk to, Mr. Raguz, and if it was prisoner of war exchanges, it was Mr. Pusic we saw. The exact relationship between Mr. Pusic and Mr. Raguz and the exact delineation of those issues, I don't know; but if I wanted to talk about prisoner of war exchanges or movements of population from Central Bosnia, it was Mr. Pusic I went to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, movements of the population, internally displaced persons and refugees, those movements were dealt with by the office headed by Mr. Raguz. We were shown a document a little while ago, 05960. You saw this document referring to the arrival of refugees from Vares, how they were received in Stolac by Mr. Herceg, the secretary of the office. Therefore, this office had the task of dealing with displaced persons and refugees, whereas Mr. Pusic dealt primarily with the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I would disagree with that. I've said Mr. Pusic, prisoners. But the difference is that he also appeared to certainly be knowledgeable and giving us information about those movements, numbers that were coming out of Central Bosnia, and when. So I don't -- all I can say is he was knowledgeable and he passed that information to us. So that's why we saw him. I did never -- what I can also say if that helps I didn't deal with Mr. Raguz on prisoner of war exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question: Mr. Alikadic's name was mentioned. You recalled it later on. Can you say something more about him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Alikadic, I think we're referring to, and he at -- certainly by the end -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Alikadic participated in some negotiations and he was on the east side representing the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You recalled his name. You mentioned it after the break.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I'm getting Alikadic and Akmadzic mixed up. My apologies. I don't have a great recollection of Mr. Alikadic. If you could point me to a document then it may refresh my mind, but I just can't pull his face or my dealings with him. I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's the person who participated in negotiations at the local level concerning exchanges of prisoners, and we saw some documents yesterday showing that both he and Mr. Pusic were present at various meetings.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that reference. It would help -- if you think we need to pursue this a little bit more, could you refer me to that document just so I can quickly refresh my mind. I now know who we're talking about broadly but I want to remember the context. Certainly when we were dealing with exchanges of prisoners with the armija, Dzumo [sic] was one of the key players and Mr. Alikadic, but it would be helpful if it you would point me to that document and then it would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dziho. For the transcript, Mr. Dziho and Mr. Alikadic, persons who participated in negotiations concerning the exchange of prisoners of war at the local level.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the two names on the - on the Muslim side that I dealt with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wish to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Praljak, and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to clarify the time. You said that the Defence had seven hours, as far as I can remember. Mr. Karnavas had two. The Defence of Mr. Petkovic and my Defence had an hour and a half, and the rest 40 minutes each. As I have been given 20 minutes by Mr. Coric's Defence and 20 minutes by Mr. Pusic's Defence and some time from Mr. Petkovic's Defence, could we please ask the registry to calculate precisely how much time I have so that I can distribute my time accordingly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will add those times up. But, in fact, you have an hour and a half, plus 20 minutes that was given to you by Mr. Coric, plus the 20 minutes that were allocated to you, so in total an hour and 70 minutes, plus Mr. Petkovic's time. So I believe that you have approximately two hours, but we shall make the calculations. We will check this during the break. So after the break it is going to be Ms. Nozica's turn. She has 40 minutes. She will start at that point. Would you like to add something, Mr. Praljak? No? Very well. So let's take a 20-minute break and we'll resume in 20 minutes' time from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. During the break the registry -- the registrar has used his computers to -- that allows me to tell Mr. Praljak that he has two hours and 20 minutes. We still have one hour today, 40 minutes for Ms. Nozica, and therefore we'll be able to conclude the day with the cross-examination of Ms. Nozica. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Watkins. And I'd like to ask the usher's assistance to hand round the binders that I'm going to start off. One binder for the witness and a binder for the Prosecution. I think Their Honours already have a set. As you can see there are quite a few documents there, but unfortunately in the short space of time of 40 minutes I'm not going to go able to get through them all, but I'll do my best to focus on what I consider to be important or -- and we'll see how far we get. I'd like to take you back to a topic that was raised on several occasions in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination, that is the establishment of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And to start off with, let me take you back to a Prosecution document, which you'll find in the Prosecution binder. And I'm going to use quite a few of the Prosecution documents, so you'll have to look through them. The number is P 06382.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's a document dated the 3rd of November, 1993, and my colleague a moment ago showed it to you, but what I'm interested in is this: The assessments and evaluations you made in your response to a question from the Prosecution with respect to the position of the minister of defence, but before we go into that, let us just take a look at a remark under M1. So after the section dealing with the parliament. It says, "M1": "M1 visited Enver Zebic." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but your colleague referred me to a different document. Just for the record, previously we were looking at 6381.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. You're quite right. And it said that: M1 visit the Emin Zebic in Jablanica who stated that the investigation on vandalism to the ECMM mission had still not been completed and that the Mujahedin were suspected as having been the perpetrators of that act. Do you remember that particular incident? There is a document about it. It is 3505976, dated the 20th of October, which talks about the incident. You don't have to look for the document but just tell me if you remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the incident, and I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under point 6. For everybody in the courtroom, P 05976 is the document number. Can you tell us what you know about this and what happened, what the incident was about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle was an armoured Mercedes and it was being driven by the team Mike 1. I know that one of the monitors was a Slovakian called Simovcek [phoen], and essentially what happened is the vehicle was stopped and the ECMM monitors were ordered out of the vehicle. I remember the -- that they were asked to stand by the side of the road, and weapons were cocked behind them. I believe they were discharged. Not at the -- the monitors, but after the discharging of the weapons, obviously to intimidate them, the vehicle was stolen. We didn't recover the vehicle then, but it was an ongoing issue which I was addressing as late at the middle of 1994 with the command of 3rd Corps armija. So that is -- this is the incident and that's the vehicle. And it was Mujahedin. Based in Konjic, we later found. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any information by which later on in some of their operations they used this vehicle of yours, precisely in order to cover up the identity and source of who they were on the ground? Did you have any knowledge to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually discovered the location of the vehicle as it was being held in Konjic, and by this time it was painted in military camouflage colours. They didn't actually hide the fact that they had it, and on one occasion had the audacity to drive to our headquarters in Zenica and pull the car into the car park, blow the horn to draw attention, and then drive off.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that they -- this was a display of might, a show of force. Would you say that? And to show that they were invincible, that nobody could do anything to them, not even your mission. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were suggestions that military action might be specifically taken against those owners of the vehicle, and those were discussed by -- with us. We, however, felt that that just might provoke the seizure of another vehicle. So I did in fact ask the corps commander, and, forgive me, his name has just temporarily gone, but it was in fact not Enver Hadzihasanovic, it was his successor. He said to me, "Your vehicle was stolen. That is a police matter. You must refer it to the police."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, at key moments when the fighting was going on in Central Bosnia and for Central Bosnia, and when there was this great expulsion of the Croatian population, when part of the Croatian population, as you yourself said, fled from the pockets where there were Croatian soldiers. Since you were there during these important times, and we have had very few a witnesses who were as high ranking and as well informed as you were, could you please briefly tell us how objective it this presence of the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia was, in your assessment, and how far did it present a problem with respect to realistic fear and the instilling of an abstract fear in the hearts and minds of the Croatian population and also the Serb population? In fact, for anybody who wasn't a Muslim at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there was a lot of confusion about numbers and also definitions as to what and who were Mujahedin, and I think I alluded earlier to our belief and our certain knowledge that there were Mujahedin who had come from outside of Bosnia, from a variety of countries, and they formed a relatively small core, and they were operating from a number of places, the area south of Zenica, and Konjic I can be specific about, and I personally had an interesting afternoon with the Mujahedin, detained by them at the village of Opera. We needn't discuss that in too much detail, but the additional element as opposed to those that we physically saw and in actually the case I saw, I'm talking about maybe five or six foreign nationals, one of African origin who spoke French, another who was wearing what I would call an Afghan headdress, I'm not sure, it's a cap, it's commonly seen there, a variety of nationals. However, there were others who were called Mujahedin and they formed brigades one was 17 Muslim brigade and I forget the other designation, and they were not from outside Bosnia. They were motivated and I would say religiously motivated, and those brigades were often used as the vanguard for attacks. Now, to come specifically to your question as to how that affected the mentality of the Bosnian Croats specifically, I can comment on that rather than the Serbs. It was significant, and the concern and fear of what would happen to an individual or to a community that was attacked by Mujahedin had a force multiplying effect. In other words, it was greater than the capability of the Mujahedin who were armed with small arms, but it had a significant impact, and on various occasions we either responded to references to where massacres had happened by the Mujahedin, and we followed those up, and in the process of doing that I did gain access with Mr. Junhov, Torbjorn Junhov who I referred to yesterday, at the period of handover as I took over the CC Travnik. There had been fighting in the villages between Zenica and Travnik, and in particular places like Guca Gora on a road there, and there had been a number of indications of Mujahedin activity, which we followed up. We were unable to establish specifically any graves resulting from a massacre, but I have no doubt that they were involved in those forces, and the effect on the population, military and civilian, that were in the Vitez pockets was significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd just like to focus on two things. The crime happened in Guca Gora; right? When you were there. I just need confirmation. Against the Croats, that is; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guca Gora was attacked. I didn't use the word "crime." I went to Guca Gora, and I was involved in the evacuation of the population that had taken refuge in the church there. This would be a good example of where we had anticipated perhaps finding significant Mujahedin activity, and we didn't.
