What we did actually find were a number of people that had been killed, but the evidence seemed to suggest that they were military HVO and they had fought, but there were also some wounded who we -- who we treated who were civilians. I didn't see the Mujahedin there, but again my estimation would have been, yes, they would have been involved in the fighting around there but I didn't see a subsequent atrocity. With regards as to whether it's a crime, well, as I say, that's a -- I saw no criminal acts. I saw military forces fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, a crime can be perpetrated also against members of the army, but let's not go into that. We'll leave that to the jurists to decide. The second point that I found interesting is this: Without a doubt, a group of Mujahedin did arrive and fought with the BH army, on the side of the BH army, but that they had members of the BH army -- that the BH army had members that adopted their religion and -- so this gave rise to greater fear. Not only the Mujahedin -- because of the Mujahedin, but also the BH army members who adopted their method of fighting, their religion, and so on, their ways. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of -- one of the characteristics of -- of the fighting in Bosnia was that people sought solace in their culture, in their religion, in their flag, and we saw extremism elements emerging. And, yes, I think it is true that the Mujahedin did have an effect, but I would also state that it was, I think, vastly exaggerated. But it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us go back to the establishment of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna now, and may we take a look at the document again. It is P 06382.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you that underneath the names of the officials a portion refers to Mr. Perica Jukic. Now, you said during the examination-in-chief that at that time it was calculated that Mr. Perica Jukic, in the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, would be the defence minister in that government. Can you confirm that already at that period of time, we're talking about the 3rd of November, that you had information to that effect already at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm -- the exact dates, I don't know. What I can confirm is that we understood Mr. Jukic was holding two posts. One was the president of the Assembly and the other was the defence minister, and that one would be relinquished. I think probably that -- that -- I don't know exactly when that happened, but certainly by the 31st of December at the Assembly meeting, and maybe just before that, if we could refer to those other documents, Mr. Jukic had become the minister of defence. I'm pretty sure I got that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll get to that shortly. Now, would you take a look at the document dated the 8th of November, 1993, and it is P 06381. It is a document shown to you by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On page 2 you have an assessment of which people could take up what posts within the government. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And under A we see Mr. Stojic's name, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic. I omitted to introduce myself at the beginning. But later on he wasn't elected defence minister. That's a fact too; right? And as far as I understand you to say, when this report was compiled, the situation was that Mr. -- it would be Perica Jukic or -- in the house of deputies, that he would occupy one of those two posts. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is why I was hesitant on -- on dates, because actually here we are still at the end of the December and I'm putting Stojic there. But we did know that there were some changes in there, but exactly the date it took place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. You placed -- you placed this document on the 8th of November. On my copies in both languages it says 3rd November. Probably I'm wrong, but you will perhaps help me to dissipate the doubts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we look at the document -- P 06381, 6381, that's the document I moved on to, 81 being the last digits. 6381. It is a document dated the 8th of November, 1993. Am I right? Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have it, but I was looking at -- at 6382, actually. That would be the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the previous document, indeed, and I've moved on to this other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I moved on to this other document to show -- and we're looking at the 8th of November. Well, this is a piece of information. We can see who compiled the report and information about these individuals. And if we can just note that the person under A, B, C, D, were not elected and did not -- were not elected to the government. Branko Stojic or Bruno Stojic, Branko Kresic, Zoran Buntic, and Mr. Neventoni. I think there's a mistake in the name, because Neventoni didn't exist. Let's go back to page 1, and under point 3 you said the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna has three political institutions, the Presidency, the government, and the house of representatives. That's what you note. Is that right, that those are the bodies that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna will have? Now, my learned friend Mr. Karnavas showed you a document yesterday when the government was appointed. It's P 06583. It is the third from the bottom in my binder. The number is P 06583.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, in the pink binder. Right. You have it. Now, there we see that the government has been named, and I am interested in the post of defence minister, Perica Jukic, on the 10th of November. Can we take note that this was two days after that report of yours?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And your prognosis about the fact that it could be him, well, he was actually appointed. Now, I'd just like to read out the number of the document, but we're not actually going to go back to it, but it was shown to you by Mr. Karnavas, and for the record I'm going to give the document number. It was P 06772, and it was an excerpt from the Official Gazette, national gazette, on the election of the president, the vice-president, and government members, and the decision was enacted on the 20th of November, which means 10 days later, after the government was appointed, was named. Now, between this naming of these people and before it was ratified that there was a meeting, a government meeting, I asked you whether you knew that there was this meeting. If not, it does not matter.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have a statement, and it was drawn out on the first day of there being an anticipated meeting when the nominations would be made, and I do remember that the first date that we mentioned slipped and it hadn't happened, but I -- so that's all I have to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we can now confirm, and this is fairly important as far as I'm concerned, that on the 10th of November the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was elected. This would follow on from the documents. And -- or, rather, appointed, and that coincides with what you said, and that Perica Jukic was appointed the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure on those dates because I'm -- I'm reading the documents and seeing the dates in front of you. My understanding was that the date on which the proposed ministerial positions were going to be adopted was delayed, and I seem to remember that it was not until into December that we had the actual ratification, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I was interested in the knowledge you had. These are documents, Prosecution documents, that haven't been challenged by anyone, so they are completely reliable, and I just wanted to see what you knew about them. And I'd like to move and now to another area, a very important area that you mentioned, and it was the structure of the authorities in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and later on the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna [as interpreted]. May I take a look at P 04431, please. It is a Prosecution document, P 0 -- just tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Now, your documents are very inspiritive, they inspire, and under point 29, for example, we had the situation with respect to prisoners, exchanged persons from Heliodrom. Paragraph 30 is a very important paragraph because of the situation in Bugojno, the visit to the prisoner camp. For the record I'm saying this. Paragraph 41 is significant, too, and I'd like to dwell on that for just a moment. Let's look at it together, and it talks with about your observation about Serbs and Croats in Vares, and here it says that on the 23rd of August it was reported that only 500 Croats left Vares via Serb-controlled territory and that 3.000 are still waiting for departure, and not a single able-bodied man was able to leave. I don't know what you think but it demonstrates that the Serbs showed goodwill where civilians were concerned, but quite obviously not when it referred to HVO members. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, could I point out that this report was not written by me. This has come from the headquarters of Zagreb. It's humanitarian activity, but it will draw on reports written by my teams. Now, specifically on that point, I -- all sorts of deals were done. I do not know specifically whether the Serbs were preventing the movement of people of male -- of males of fighting age through there or whether in fact it was the authorities within Vares that wouldn't let them go, because of course that would have weakened their own ability to defend.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Watkins, I believe the source of this report, where it says the Serbs did not allow them to do that, but not to dwell on that. Now, I wanted to ask you about cooperation between the Muslim side and the Serbs, but we'll go into that with someone else in due course. But I'd just like to focus on paragraph 34 and the Prosecutor asked you about that. It is the decision to release a certain number of Muslims from the camp, and what I'd actually like to see is what your knowledge and information was about the position of, let's say, a mayor, because you said yesterday during in-chief that people had different positions, that the heads of the civilian or civic authorities had a different position in Central Bosnia from what they did in the south and in Herzegovina. And now I'd like to ask you: Do you know that the presidents of the municipalities on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were simultaneously members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say the top-most body, the top-most authority in Herceg-Bosna? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understood that most of them took positions or would be taking positions in the new emerging Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We're talking about the period before the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and after the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, in order to see the realistic it power they had, let us take a look at the next document, which is P 00079 in my binder. It's the first document in that binder.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just refer -- before I go back to that last question because I think I may have gone off on a slightly different -- I was aware that mayors had a constitutional role in the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you'll remember that on Monday I made reference to that as part of bringing legitimacy to the later formed Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna that was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. We're not talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina or the constitutional position, because it's quite clear to the Trial Chamber that neither the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna or Community of Herceg-Bosna had a constitution. They regulated their relationships with acts, which are not the same as a constitution, and these acts show that they were part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not an independent or autonomous state. But with respect to the positions of the Presidency or, rather, the mayor, I'd like to ask you something about that, and this is an important question, and you gave rise to it by saying that their position depended on -- upon somebody in Mostar. So it's a complex question to understand, that the president of a municipality is in the bodies of the authorities somewhere towards the bottom, subordinated to the government, but at the same time that mayor is a member of the Presidency. So let's take a look at this document. And you don't have to know about this, but I'd just like us to understand what the position is and why the presidents of the municipalities had far greater authority than one would assume, if one didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have your -- I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I don't know whether you've ever had this document in your hands because it's very significant, you know, to understand the aspirations, reasons, goals, motives. Have you ever seen it before? It's the 18th of November, 1991. Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please let's just look at point 7 together -- or, rather, Article 7, which says that, "the top leadership of the community shall consist of the Presidency which shall consist of representatives of the Croatian people in the municipal government and the senior members or presidents of the municipal boards of the Croatian Democratic Union. "The Presidency shall elect a president, two vice-presidents, and a secretary." "The Presidency shall elect ..." They were the ones who elected Mr. Mate Boban, so you can see how important they are. This document has the signatories, and to see who these are, let's look at P 00081. It's the identical document. In the Croatian version you have the same decision, and in the English version you have the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just wanted to note an objection, with all respect to my learned friend. Is seems like we've gone back to simply reading documents to the witness. Last series of questions now for some minutes and I've been following the transcript quite closely, counsel has just read a number of documents and there has been no question or no affirmation or no evidentiary value added by the witness. We're simply reading documents and then going on to the next document, and you can see that on the page we just left. Point out a document and let's go to the next document. There's no questions. It's simply reading documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica. You are introducing documents, but you have to ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by Mr. Scott's leave, I will, but the witness must first see all the documents in order for me to be able to put a question. I explained quite clearly to the Court why I was doing this. I'm doing it because of what the witness said yesterday as to position of the president of the municipality. If you allow me to show the document that completes this series, I'll put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Witness, have you found P 00081? It's the second one in the binder.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On page 2, if you'll just turn the page, you will find the signatures of the mayors who supported -- or, rather, enacted this decision is. For example, 27, Capljina, the mayor we referred to when talking about release from prison, Mr. Pero Markovic. I'm almost sure it's his signature. I can't be absolutely sure, but it looks like his, and there's no doubt he was there. Could we please look at one more document before we establish what the actual position of mayors was so that we can say what kind of powers they had. It's P 0596, the third document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't delve into it very deeply. Let's just look at Article 33 together. That's page 6 in English. It's the rule of procedure of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of the 17th of October, 1992 and published in the Official Gazette of November 1992. In Article 33, let's see what the powers of the Presidency are. Although you're not a lawyer, I'll just briefly refer you to Article 33 too, and it says that, "appointments, nominations, excuse of -- or, rather, implementation of acts and other documents --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down in reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Through its conclusion the Presidency of the HZ HB will determine viewpoints and opinions on matters discussed to determine the main guidelines for the work and tasks of the HVO ..." So they are the ones establishing or determining the guidelines for the work of the government not covered by this, these rules of procedure. And let's look at Article 40. That's page 7 in English. Can you please look at the powers? It says: "There the Presidency of the HZ HB evaluates that regulation or piece of legislation issued by the HV HZ HB is contrary to one issued by the Presidency, it will require it to be harmonised or brought into line or for other measures to be instituted within a given time limit. "If the HVO HZ HB should not act in accordance with the previous paragraph, the Presidency of HZ HB shall annul such acts and order that a new one be introduced." Sir, I have two other documents here, one referring to the mayors after the establishment of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which you spoke about. I know you have not seen these documents before, but had you known that these were the powers of the mayors or presidents of municipalities, first of all, would you agree that in the period up to the establishment of the republic they had legislative powers? We see that the Presidency issues acts, can annul acts, so that formally in the hierarchy it's above the HZ HB government. Would you agree with me, at least on the basis of what we have just read? If you doubt what I have just read, please say so. I know you are not a lawyer, but simply you are the one who ascribed to them certain -- a certain position saying that they were under the influence of the authorities in Mostar, but what I'm trying to show you is that they were in fact the highest authority. So would you agree that this is what follows from these documents and did you have any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of these documents, and as you've taken me through, I can see the -- the importance. I have never doubted the importance of the -- the mayors. I spent a lot of time meeting them to understand what was going on. But by the time I arrived there, this document, for instance, 00596, this does relate to the constitution of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and what I was exploring was the change, the period of fluidity, what their new responsibilities would be, and I'm sure as their -- the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed of course reference would have been made to what had been there before. It would be very strange if it wasn't, and it would be very strange if this document had an influence. But in the period I arrive, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna doesn't exist. A new structure is being formed, and in that I am trying to understand what the particular powers are. My point yesterday about the ability of a mayor to act independently was really to contrast what -- what the situation was like in Central Bosnia where there wasn't such a reach of government and an ability to, if you like, impose any sanction on anyone whose powers went beyond that established in the constitution, and my reference to the importance of the mayors in the Hercegovina territory was simply by contrast, that I felt it very unlikely that they could do -- be too independent of what the key leaders in government - and by that I would refer to Mate Boban and Jadranko Prlic and so on - they would not have major discretion. There would be -- if they were doing things that didn't fit with what was happening in a war period, then there would have been means by which pressure or influence could be brought to bear on them by contrast to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, certainly the situation in Central Bosnia differed if for no other reason than for that of communication, but doesn't the opposite follow from the documents I showed you, that they were able to exert pressure on the government rather than vice versa? However, if you know nothing about this, there are documents to show this, and there will be other witnesses to testify about it. However, I would now like to move on to another area very briefly. My time, however, seems to have run out. If Mr. Praljak would like to continue -- thank you. Thank you. We will now move on to a different question. Today my colleague Mr. Karnavas showed you a document, but you probably don't have the binder before you. It's P 05709. Just listen, please, and you will remember very easily what this is about. It's a report by Mr. Martin Garrod. You'll probably remember what it's about. And in that document -- well, now you will have it on your screen. P 05 -- yes. Thank you. You are the fastest witness we've had so far in finding documents. So this is a document dated the 7th of October, 1993. At that time, as regards the political options of the -- let's call it government in Sarajevo or Muslim government, you said that the political option was a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, but does it follow from this document that there was another political option, possibly the establishment of a separate Muslim entity or state, and that there was a split between what the army wanted and what the political leadership wanted at that point in time? Was that your impression in October and November in your contacts with military and political representatives of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly came across those differences of opinion as to whether the battle, the fighting, was about maintaining the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its existing boundaries, or whether these options of there being smaller republics as an issue to be explored, and there definitely were differences between military commanders who we had discussions with and some of the political leadership. And just on that point, on military commanders, a name I couldn't remember earlier with reference to the Mujahedin it was Sakib Mahmuljin. It's just come to me. So yes, there were differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we clarify this a little bit? Was the army more in favour of taking everything by military means and having control over all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while the politicians were a little more pragmatic and accepted other options also? I'm having a problem with interpretation. They may have misheard me. Was it your impression that the army aspired or tried to persuade everyone that they could take the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by military means, while politicians were a little more pragmatic and considered options that might lead to the establishment of an entity of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have dealt in generalisms earlier and I think I've been guilty myself of using them but I think that is broad. One thing I could say about the armija commanders is there was a pretty shrewd and realistic assessment of their military capability. And I don't think if you were in 3rd Corps headquarters or 2nd Corps headquarters you really believed that you would be able to take large amounts of territory. Certainly some to gain tactical advantage, and we saw that, but not to reclaim all of the territory by military force and I think the reality of their ability to do that. They were well equipped in numbers of people, but they were lightly equipped in weapons and heavy weapons. So it would have been a very unrealistic assessment, and most the corps commanders had JNA background and I think they would have realised that whatever intent that they might have personally, that it would not be achievable in the way that you described. Some -- some certainly would have had that, but I think there was a shrewd assessment that it couldn't be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to go into military matters because that's not my area of expertise, and Mr. Praljak will be putting more questions about that, but there's something that seems significant to me here. You dealt with what weapons the HVO had, and you've just said that the army of BH compensated for the lack of weapons by large numbers of men. So could we say that the armija had far more men than the HVO had?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the received which is come that, the one advantage, or two advantages, that the armija had, one was that it had an advantage in manpower. The other one was always related to their morale being high.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, when you mention "morale," I'd like to go back to the Mujahedin, but I won't go into that. Let's go back to my original questions. Please look at P 06693. It's in the Prosecutor's binder. P 06693. P 06693.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so fast at finding the documents without the assistance of the Court. I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I was too quick in praising you. Let's look at English page 2. For the sake of the record, it's a special report, Geneva 6 -- 16th, November 1993, and on page 2 in the English version we have under B, "Muslim goals." As for the goals of the Muslim politicians and army, I put questions to you about that because they are mentioned in this report. You can see it before you, but I'll refer only to a part. As Kordic properly pointed out, "One might say that the Muslim leadership itself has not decided what its final and ultimate goal is. Do they want ethnic separation along ethnic lines, and if so, within what territory?" Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I think that's a correct assessment, and I think that could be applied to others involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just let me finish. So the option is either an ethnic entity or a unitary state covering all of BH, but in the next paragraph it says: "However, if the former Minister of Foreign Affairs, Silajdzic, who is thought capable of persuading his fellow politicians were to become Prime Minister, this might mean that the current balance between the two options could weigh on the side of ethnic separation along ethnic lines." Mr. Silajdzic was actually appointed Prime Minister. Would we agree on that? But let's just look at what the standpoint of the army was. Two passages lower down, it says: "Of course we also heard dissenting opinions on this matter, more specifically from the commander of the 3rd BH army corps and his aide, who do not believe in the partition solution, but who declare that they will obey and carry out the orders issued by the politicians." Mr. Watkins, we can see from this that on the 16th of November, a political assessment had been made where the Muslim side, and I don't have time to explain now why I say the Muslim side, but you refer to it in the same way, the Muslim side had two options. The whole of Bosnia, if we can get it; a separate republic, if we can't, whereas the army said, "We don't agree, but we will comply with the political decisions." Is that what follows from this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly speaking I would accept that characterisation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I will show you one more document on the same topic, and that will be the last one. That's P 03771. It's also a Prosecution document, and you have already been shown it by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I -- just before going on to that document, and I'm sorry, it's -- when I said, "broadly speaking," I do broadly accept what was said, but it may just be helpful. You said very specifically that "the whole of Bosnia, if we can get it," and what I would agree to in that statement is maintenance of the integrity of the borders with a central government operating out of Sarajevo. I would not draw, and I'm not saying you were asking me to draw the conclusion, that it would be a state entirely controlled by the Muslims. I just want to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, at the point in time we are talking about, more than half of that state was in the hands of the Serbs. Republika Srpska was in existence. We are referring to the 16th of November. Was it possible to take control over the entire territory in any other way? Let's take the Serbs as an example. I am referring now to November, because the NATO strikes pushed them a little back later. I was a little confused. But if the Serbs are holding 70 per cent of the territory at that point how could the central authorities in Sarajevo have control over the entire territory unless they defeated the Serbs by military means? I will not discuss with you the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what the central government represented, because that is a topic we would need a lot of time for, and who at that point in time was part of the central government? Who represented the Serbs and the Croats? Were there only Muslims there? Was their Presidency elected legitimately or not? There are many issues that arise here, but all I'm asking you is to tell me whether, if the political leaders from Sarajevo at that time wanted control over all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did that mean military conquest, or liberation, if you want to call it that, of at least the territory held by the Serbs at that time? There's another interesting document on this topic. My time is really running out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you not answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not answer yet. I was just re-reading, because I don't know whether it is just something that I'm not clear on the question. All I was doing by going back to the question that you -- you placed to me, and I broadly agreed, was that we have been discussing today about the territorial ambitions of Muslim forces, and I'm simply saying that I agree with you that the options that were being discussed were either a -- a control over an area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which they would have military control or a complete Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm just clarifying that by agreeing with you on those two points that I'm not suggesting that there was a military ambition to control the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Clearly they could not have defeated the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. Now let's finally look at a document referring to some political thinking of the leaders in Sarajevo. P 03771. Just tell me when you have found it and we'll deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Point 4, BritBat sector, A Vitez, B, Novi Travnik. Just tell me when you've found that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we have a conversation with Mr. Alagic. You'll know who Mr. Alagic is. Can you tell Their Honours? It was in your territory. The document is dated the 28th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th of July. The -- he was either still in 3rd Corps or 7th Corps had been established and he became the commander of 7th corps. I forget the exact dates, but I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we can say General Alagic, he was a general at the time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure at this time he would have been the general in command of 7th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll just refer you to the second sentence where it says: "In further conversations, Alagic expressed little faith in the political leadership and said that Bosnia-Herzegovina should continue -- would continue to fight for a Bosnia and was critical of Izetbegovic's identification of the struggle for a Muslim state." It follows from this that Mr. Alagic, a general in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as early as in July 1993 spoke about Mr. Izetbegovic's aspiration to create a Muslim state. This document confirms it. Mr. Alagic disagreed with it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had similar conversations with myself with Mr. Alagic over whisky, which wasn't traditionally something which you would expect an extremist Muslim to be sharing with me. He had his own issues with the involvement of Mujahedin in the area, and he disagreed with quite a few people and quite a few politicians, but what I wouldn't agree was at this stage Mr. Izetbegovic was trying to pursue a Muslim state. That's my personal impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just my last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't expect you to agree with that. All I wanted to do was to show you what Mr. Alagic felt about it. I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Judges for allowing me to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute and 40 seconds we went over our time. Thank you very much, and I would like to remind all of you that we will resume this hearing tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
